Short title: EEA: Malta among highest fossil-fuel subsidies relative to GDP
Claim and who made it: European Environment Agency (indicator page, 29 Jan 2025): in 2023 fossil-fuel subsidies represented the highest shares of GDP in Malta, Poland and Slovakia, all at or above 1.5%.
Counter-evidence or context: The ranking reproduces exactly from the Commission's subsidy database (2024 edition) that the EEA used, and holds with Eurostat GDP (as of 6 Oct 2026, which the EEA could not have had) and, as a lower bound, with the unconfirmed items set to zero; but Slovakia's "at or above 1.5%" holds only on the EEA's basis (1.507%; 1.49% with Eurostat GDP; 1.39% with the unconfirmed items set to zero). Malta's 2023 figure (EUR 605m, or 633m with a stand-in) is 96% one line, compensation to Enemalta for frozen energy prices, booked as actual costs and wholly to natural gas; it is 2.1 times the IMF Article IV energy-subsidy cost for 2023 (1.4% of GDP, CR 26/29) and 1.7 times the Government's expected cost (1.7% of GDP, DBP 2024, other basic commodities included), a gap we could not reconcile. For 2022 the database was lower (1.71% of GDP, the line EUR 246.6m) than the Government (2.5%, about EUR 451m) and the IMF (1.8%, about EUR 325m); over 2022-23 the line (EUR 826.5m) is close to the Government's expected cost (about EUR 806m), which points to timing or basis; the 2024 gap (about 1.8% against 0.87%) persists. The IMF's price-gap database records no explicit subsidy for Malta; the OECD/IISD tracker has no OECD or IEA estimate for Malta. Malta was 0.08-0.10% of GDP in 2015-2020 (24th-27th of 27) and is first again for 2024 in COM(2026) 472. In euros Malta's EUR 0.63bn is 19th of 27.
Test it against: Commission subsidy inventory 2024 edition (CIRCABC) rebuilt measure by measure (locally); EEA chart data; COM(2025) 17 Figure 16 (read by pixel); Eurostat nama_10_gdp, gov_10a_main and nrg_cb_e; Malta Draft Budgetary Plans 2024 and 2025; IMF CR 26/29 Table 2 (read for CC-018/CC-022); IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Data 2023 update; OECD/IISD Fossil Fuel Subsidy Tracker; COM(2026) 472; ECFIN Discussion Paper 214 for definitions (tools/cc-113-report/calc.py).
Why it is low-hanging: A single threshold claim in an open EEA dataset, which also links to the energy-subsidy claims already in the collection.
Caveats: Statement by an EU agency about EU data; the EEA states its definition (WTO categories, EU inventory method). The claim is about shares of GDP (in euros Malta is 19th of 27). 2023 values are provisional for the items still to be confirmed (about 7-8% of the EU total; in Malta only the EUR 28.2m excise cut); Malta's EUR 580m line is booked as actual costs and is not reconciled with other sources. Versions C and D (unconfirmed items set to zero) are a lower bound, not equally valid versions; B and D use Eurostat GDP as of 6 Oct 2026, which the EEA could not have had. COM(2025) 17 (28 Jan 2025) was read from the EU Publications Office: its Figure 16 gives the same top four as the CIRCABC file, which was modified on 9 Apr 2025. The Commission workbook is (c) Enerdata (reproduction prohibited without written permission): measure rows are not committed. The original 29 Jan 2025 page could not be opened; the earliest copy read is 3 Feb 2025. IMF CR 26/29 figures are from the CC-018/CC-022 record (read in full 5 Oct 2026). Largely supported verdict: no right of reply needed.

Short title: PN: only EU state with rising emissions intensity
Claim and who made it: Nationalist Party press release signed by Shadow Minister Eve Borg Bonello (26 Jan 2026; in Maltese, our translation), citing Eurostat: "Malta is the only EU Member State which, instead of reducing, increased the intensity of greenhouse gas emissions from 2013 to date. Malta in fact increased these emissions by 17%, when the average intensity of these emissions in all EU Member States fell by 34%"; "In simple words, it is not simply that we are polluting more because the economy grew, but today, for every euro we put into our economy, we are polluting more than we were polluting in 2013"; and "This is the direct result of a lack of ambition on the part of the Maltese Government on several fronts. Among them, the clear lack of ambition to seriously increase the use of renewable energy." The release also says Estonia "reduced emissions by 64%", Ireland "by 50%" and Finland "by 44%", and that Malta generated "only 10.7%" of its energy from renewables in 2024 when the European average is "a little over 25%", "third from last".
Counter-evidence or context: Eurostat's figure is quoted correctly (January release +16.6%, EU -34.0%; August 2026 data +14.3%, still the only rise; Malta 27th of 27 from every base year 2008-2023; EU-27 values flagged i), but it is a residence-based measure. Malta's resident production units emitted 2.78 Mt CO2e in 2013 and 6.59 Mt in 2024; air transport rose from 0.30 to 4.73 Mt (71.8% of 2024), 116% of the net increase; all of the rise is fuel bought abroad by resident air transport firms (Eurostat bridging table: 299 of 304 kt in 2013, 100% of the 2024 estimate). The NSO attributes the 2023 jump to airlines that started operating that year. Without air-transport emissions the indicator fell from every base year 2008-2023 (-8.5% to -72%): -64.0% since 2013 (2nd-largest fall in the EU; EU -35.2%) but -29.5% since 2016 (17th of 27; EU -30.1%). The territorial inventory per euro of GDP also fell from every base year (-6.6% to -69%): -61.3% since 2013 (2nd after Estonia; EU -35.5%), -27.1% since 2016 (21st; EU -29.8%). Most of the fall came in 2014-2016, when electricity-sector emissions fell from 1,703 to 581 kt (743 kt in 2024, +28% since 2016), so these counter-figures depend on the base year too; in the PN's favour, from base years 2014-2019 Malta's rise is +19.5% to +97%. The renewables explanation does not fit: with zero electricity-sector emissions in 2024 the indicator would still be 1.4% above 2013 (329.8 against 325.2 g/EUR), and renewable shares rose over the period (electricity 1.6% to 10.7%, overall 3.8% to 17.2%). The release's next paragraph also cites traffic; households' own car use is outside the indicator and land transport firms went from 49 to 86 kt. With 2013 as base Malta is the only riser only for end year 2024, a Eurostat estimate; 2013-2023 it fell 8.3% and no state rose. Estonia, Ireland and Finland cut intensity, not emissions: residence accounts / territorial inventory 2013-2024, Estonia -55.4% / -53.1% (2024 flagged i), Finland -37.9% / -37.6% (i), Ireland +13.7% / -6.9% (flagged e; its air transport, 9.90 to 16.32 Mt, is 87% of its residence-based rise). 10.7% is Malta's renewable share of electricity (EU 47.5%); its overall share is 17.2%, fourth from last (EU 25.2%); Eurostat's release of 18 Dec 2025 named Belgium, Luxembourg and Ireland as the lowest three. In the PN's favour: the statistic is real and Eurostat's own news item gives no explanation either; Malta's renewable shares are among the EU's lowest.
Test it against: Eurostat env_ac_aeint_r2 for all EU-27 (2013-2024, both vintages, start- and end-year sensitivity, and our own counter-figures from every base year 2008-2023); env_ac_ainah_r2 by activity and env_ac_aibrid_r2 for Malta's drivers; env_air_gge with nama_10_gdp for the territorial inventory per euro of GDP (and CC-025's 2005 base); nama_10_pe per person; nrg_ind_ren for the renewables figures. Recomputed in tools/cc-114-report/calc.py (data/cc-114/checks.csv, ranking_2013_2024.csv, sensitivity.csv, sensitivity_base_years.csv).
Why it is low-hanging: A clear 'only member state' ranking that open Eurostat data settle by calculation.
Data readiness: High: Eurostat and Crossref reachable; Newsbook readable.
Caveats: An opposition claim, held to the same standard and data as the Government's (CC-025): our own counter-figures are tested from every base year, as the PN's is. Translation of the Maltese release is ours. Malta's 2024 values in the air emissions accounts are Eurostat estimates (flag i); the rise since 2013 depends on them. The airlines behind Malta's air-transport series are not identified (Eurostat and the NSO name none; no company filings read). The release page was modified on 24 Apr 2026 and no January copy was found; Newsbook's quotes of 26 Jan match its text. MaltaToday's report was not readable (403). Newsbook's own additions (the 81.6% per unit of GDP since 2005, a 142% overshoot of the 2030 effort-sharing target, 24.5% renewables by 2030) are not the PN's and are not checked here; the 10.7% and "third from last" are the PN's own. "A lack of ambition on several fronts" is a political judgement and is not rated; only the renewables link is. The "Selective metric" tag means a metric favourable to the speaker's argument, not to Malta or any party. Reviewed on 6 Oct 2026 before circulation; version unchanged. Misleading: pending right of reply from the Nationalist Party; must not be circulated beyond the site before the reply deadline.

Claim and who made it: UNESCO World Heritage Committee (2025 state-of-conservation decision, as reported): Malta's current planning policies and regulations do not sufficiently safeguard Valletta's setting; the Committee asked for effective height controls within and around the property, a further-developed buffer zone, and an updated conservation report by 1 December 2026.
Counter-evidence or context: The Government treated the later deadline as a sign of confidence in its heritage management and rejected the Opposition's 'alarmism' (Lovin Malta, reported); the PN asked for a local-plan revision (MaltaToday). The Planning Authority's Floor Area Ratio policy and height rules are the policies at issue.
Test it against: UNESCO decision text and State of Conservation report; Malta's Floor Area Ratio policy, North Harbour and Grand Harbour Local Plans, the Views and Vistas Analysis; Heritage Impact Assessments for Manoel Island and other major schemes; actual permitted heights near Valletta (PA permits).
